args.text:
Screen row 0 is the status line. InitStatusLine ($544C) fills rows 0-1 from txtStatusLineTemplate ($90F8), 61 chars:
  "  PLAYER ONE  0000000  NEXT ZONE 00 KM  " then "  NEUTRONIUM STATUS  H"
So the score is the 7 digits at $040E-$0414 (scoreField+1..+7), which is exactly what CheckHighScore ($5544) compares. Colour RAM for the screen is screen+$D400 (see PrintCharAt $883A).

Difficulty loop counter. Incremented at $9DA4 when all 42 zones are cleared and clamped to 5 at $9DAD, so the game gets harder five times and then stops getting harder. Also read at $9701 to shorten a timer: $43 = 12 - 2*loopNumber.
Current zone, 0-41. Compared with #$2A at $9DA0, which is what fixes the game at 42 zones.

Screen row address tables, low bytes at $0340 and high bytes at $0360, used by ScreenAddrFromRow. They live in the tape buffer and are BUILT AT RUNTIME by sub_87FE, so the loaded image has nothing useful here - reading $0340 through this project shows whatever the decruncher left behind, not the table.

27 entries, $0400 stepping by 40. Entries 25 and 26 point past the screen at $07E8 and $0810.

The two digits of "NEXT ZONE nn KM" on the status line - offsets 33 and 34 of txtStatusLineTemplate. $9D2C decrements them as you travel ($9D35 DEC $0422, borrowing into $0421); $937B sets and carries them the other way. When they reach zero the zone is complete.

THE NEUTRONIUM STATUS BAR, on screen row 1 from column 21. Always addressed as $043C,X or $043C,Y with a 1-based index, so the first cell is $043D.

Why that address: InitStatusLine ($544C) copies $3D = 61 bytes from txtStatusLineTemplate ($90F8) into $0400, which is row 0 (40 chars) plus the first 21 of the second panel line at $9120 - so it fills $0400-$043C exactly and the bar starts at the next byte.

Eight sites move it and they are the self-modifying ones beryl found: $9C12 and $9EB8 among them have their OPCODE poked by $C023/$C046, so a static read of INC/DEC there tells you the addressing mode and not the direction. $9C0C grows it, $9EB6 shrinks it.

THE NEUTRONIUM BAR - the game main resource, and it is stored NOWHERE ELSE. It lives in screen memory: $043D to $044E, eighteen cells, row 1 columns 21-38, right under the words NEUTRONIUM STATUS. $043C is the base the code indexes 1-based.

That is why $9FAC fills it by writing #$48 to $043C,X for X = 1..$12, and why $9120 carries exactly eighteen H characters and $915E exactly eighteen colour bytes. Three independent places agree on eighteen.

A cell holds a glyph between $48 and $50 - nine states of the same bar segment in the custom charset - and $20 when empty. DrainNeutronium at $9C0C advances one cell per call and empties it when it passes $50; $4A neutroniumLeft is the index of the cell currently being eaten, so it doubles as how much is left.

Storing a resource in the display rather than in a variable is not a shortcut here, it is the whole design: the bar IS the number, and every routine that changes it does so by reading and writing screen RAM.

THE WHOLE SCREEN LAYOUT, put together from five places that each know one row of it. Screen $0400, colour $D800, 40x25.

  row 0     $0400  status line: "  PLAYER ONE  0000000  NEXT ZONE 00 KM  "
                   score = seven ASCII digits at $040E-$0414
                   distance = two digits at $0421-$0422
  row 1     $0428  "  NEUTRONIUM STATUS  " then the 18-cell fuel bar at $043D-$044E
  rows 2-11        sky. The twelve stars live here - starInitRow at $8A1A is 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 02 0B 06 07 08, all inside this band
  rows 9-10 $0590  messageLine, where BEASTS REMAINING and the zone banner are printed
  rows 14-19 $0630 $0658 $0680 $06A8 $06D0 $06F8  THE SCROLLING TERRAIN, six rows, shifted one column left by the loop at $8C53 with their colour rows $DA30-$DAF8 alongside
  rows 20-24 $0720  ground, filled with character $28 in colour 6 by the loop at $8AC6

The six terrain rows and the five ground rows are why $D016 has CSEL cleared at $8871 - 38 columns opens the side border so a column can be shifted in without showing the seam. The fine scroll is $1F counting 7 down to 0 and the coarse shift happens when it wraps, at $8C4D.

Sprites are drawn over all of it and the camel walks on the boundary at row 20.

(Added beside basalt earlier note rather than replacing it.)

First of the six scrolling terrain rows: $0630 $0658 $0680 $06A8 $06D0 $06F8, rows 14-19, with colour rows $DA30 $DA58 $DA80 $DAA8 $DAD0 $DAF8. The loop at $8C53 copies each one byte left across all 39 columns, both character and colour, once every eight frames when the fine scroll at $1F wraps. New columns are pushed in at the right by EmitTerrainColumn from newColumnChars ($1FF0).

camelMode - the player state machine, complete. ControlCamel reads the joystick only in mode 0; every other mode runs an animation in $94F6 and ignores the stick.

  0  on the ground. Left/right walk, up starts a jump, down starts a duck, fire shoots.
  1  airborne. jumpVelocity ($39) counts $0F down through $00 to $F0 and is added to objYPos as a SIGNED value, so sixteen steps up and sixteen down. At $F0 the camel lands: voice 3 gets a short triangle thud, mode becomes 5 and jumpVelocity is reset to 5.
  5  landing squash. jumpVelocity counts 4,3,2,1 and the sprite shape comes from the four bytes at $9565 - CE CF CF CE - so the camel compresses and springs back. At zero the shape returns to $C0 and the mode to 0.
  2  ducking down. INC the sprite shape until it reaches $D2, then mode 3.
  3  held down. Stays here until the player releases down, or until objXPos reaches $11, the left wall.
  4  standing up. DEC the sprite shape back to $CD, then shape $C0, mode 0, and clear objMoveType.

So the whole animation vocabulary is a contiguous run of sprite blocks: $C0 standing, $C0-$CC the walk cycle stepped by $8C2F, $CD jumping, $CE-$D2 the duck, and $CE/$CF again for the landing squash.

Firing is allowed in modes 0, 1 and 5 and refused in 2, 3 and 4 - you cannot shoot while crouched.

args.name: activeSpriteBank
args.comment: Sprite blocks $20-$3F, the ones the game swaps. CopyCharSetToRAM/$5007 copies a 2K bank here from $1000, $1800, $4000 or $4800 according to the index the wave descriptor supplies in $02. The bytes sitting here in the runtime image are whichever bank was live when the snapshot was taken.

args.name: spriteBank0
args.comment: 2K sprite bank, 32 blocks of 64 bytes. Rendered: the camel, in walk-cycle frames. One of the sources CopyCharSetToRAM/$5007 copies to $0800-$0FFF.

args.name: spriteBank1
args.comment: Sprite data. Rendered: creatures and ships. Note this bank runs out at $1D00 where the object variables begin, so only about 20 of its 32 blocks hold pictures — a copy of the full 2K from $1800 would drag variables along behind them, into blocks $3A-$3F, which nothing appears to display.

args.name: objectAndSpriteVariables
args.comment: Not graphics: 768 bytes of game state, 336 instructions reference it. Type templates, live object slots and the sprite multiplexer arrays. See the comments at $1D00, $1E40 and $1F40. It sits here because the VIC bank is $0000-$3FFF and these are sprite blocks $74-$7F, which the game simply never displays.

args.name: characterSet
args.comment:
The game font, and it is HALF a character set: 128 glyphs at $2000-$23FF, not the 2K the VIC could address from here.

$D018 = $18 at $8AE7 puts the character base at $2000. I rendered it: chunky 8x8 glyphs, A-Z at screen codes $01-$1A, digits at $30-$39, punctuation in $20-$3F. Every text table in the program is screen codes for this font, which is why $52 and $56 turn up mid-word in the messages — they are glyphs this font defines and the standard set does not.

CORRECTED after reading the zone data. I first declared this region 2K, up to $2800. It is not: the zone records use sprite blocks $90-$9F, and those are $90*64 = $2400 to $27FF. Rendering $2400 as sprites gives a walking creature in three frames; rendering it as characters gives nothing. So the upper half of what the VIC would call the character set is sprite data, which is fine because the game never writes a screen code above $7F.

args.name: residentSprites
args.comment:
7K of sprite data, blocks $90-$FF, and every zone uses it.

These are NOT in the bank table at $502F and do not need to be: the VIC bank is $0000-$3FFF, so anything from $0800 to $3FFF is reachable by a sprite pointer directly. That is exactly why the table exists — $4000 and $4800 are OUTSIDE the bank, so a set kept there has to be copied down to $0800-$0FFF first.

How the split works, read off the zone records. Every one of the 42 zones draws its creatures from blocks $20-$3F, which is the SWAPPED bank at $0800-$0FFF, plus blocks in this range, which are always there. So the resident set is the shared vocabulary — explosions at $EC-$EE appear in all 42 zones — and the swapped bank is what makes zone 30 look different from zone 3.

Starts at $2400 rather than $2800: blocks $90-$9F live in what would otherwise be the top half of the character set. Rendered, they are a walking creature.

args.name: spriteBank2
args.comment: Sprite data, out of VIC reach at $4000, so it is copied to $0800 by $5007 when a wave asks for it. Rendered as hires it comes out dithered #.#. all over, which is the signature of MULTICOLOUR sprite data read one bit per pixel: these are two-bit-per-pixel shapes.

args.name: spriteBank3
args.comment: Sprite data, out of VIC reach, copied to $0800 by $5007. Rendered: explosion or effect shapes and some letter-shaped sprites.

args.name: srcResidueSpriteSet
args.comment: Leftover assembler source, BASIC line format. See the comment at $5870.

args.name: srcResidueNexini
args.comment: Leftover assembler source. Overwritten at runtime by player one status line, which only reaches $5F27.

args.name: srcResidueMainLoop
args.comment: Leftover assembler source: MLOOP JSR STARF / JSR BULITZ / JSR CCAMEL.

args.name: zoneDataTable
args.comment: 42 zone records of 200 bytes. See the comment at $6700 for the layout and the comment on each record for its name.

args.name: padBeforeCode
args.comment: 32 zero bytes then 14 x $EA. The wave table ends at $87CF and code begins at $87FE; this is the gap. The $EA run is NOP filler rather than data anyone reads — nothing references it and it decodes to fourteen NOPs falling into the routine at $87FE.

args.name: deadReadCharAt
args.comment: JSR ScreenAddrFromRow / LDA ($48),Y - the body of a read-character-at routine whose entry point is gone. The RTS after it at $8839 is live: PrintCharAt branches there when the column is off screen.

args.name: deadRasterReload
args.comment: Five orphaned bytes, A9 60 8D 12 D0 = LDA #$60 / STA $D012. Nothing branches here: the JMP at $88FB goes over it and the music player continues at $8903. Setting the raster back to $60 is what the phase dispatcher at $8BC9 now does, so this is the old version left in place when that moved. Declared code so it reads as what it is rather than as five stray bytes.

args.name: starSeedTables
args.comment: Three 12-byte tables read 1-based: column at $8A0E, row at $8A1A, colour at $8A26, then titleFlashColours at $8A32.

args.name: terrainProfiles
args.comment: Two hill profiles for the scrolling landscape: six frames at $8DF4, ten at $8E24, six bytes of screen codes each plus two unused. See the comment at $8DF4.

args.name: moveHandlerTable
args.comment:
Three movement handlers as ordinary lo/hi pairs. sub_993A doubles the index and reads $9933,Y for the low byte and $9934,Y for the high one.

  entry 0 -> $9939, which is the $60 IMMEDIATELY AFTER this table. A byte doubling as an RTS: movement type 0 does nothing.
  entry 1 -> $994F  MoveObjectLinear
  entry 2 -> $99C0  MoveObjectAccelerating

The index is objMoveType,X AND #$7F, so bit 7 of that byte is free for something else — and the player uses it for facing ($9492 and $94A3 write $00 and $80 there).

$994C is JMP ($0002): the walk cannot follow a vector, which is why 103 instructions below it were invisible. $02/$03 is the print-column scratch pair being borrowed as a jump vector. Marking the two targets recovered them all.

args.name: messageFlashColours
args.comment: Eight colours - 00 06 02 04 05 03 07 01 - cycled into messageLineColour ($D990) by $9D13, indexed by $4F counting down. Entry 0 is black, so the message fades to invisible on the last step before $9D29 clears the line.

args.name: tailFiller
args.comment: Seventeen bytes between the last routine and $A000, where BASIC ROM takes over. 90 00 FF 10 00 00 00 FF 00 80 00 18 43 42 4F 4F 16 - the tail reads CBOO in PETSCII, so this is most likely residue from the build machine like the assembler source at $5870, not data. Nothing references it and no code reaches it. I cannot tell what it was.

args.name: underBasicRom
args.comment:
8192 bytes of zero in the image, and never read as RAM.

Nothing in this program writes $00 or $01, so the 6510 port stays at its power-on $37 and BASIC ROM is banked in across $A000-$BFFF. Every read of this range — NextRandom at $8D21, and TitleColourAndSoundStep at $50BD — gets ROM, not these bytes.

Declared data so it stops showing as unexplained. It is explained: it is a window onto ROM that this project cannot model, because a layer supplying an address always wins and nothing has loaded a KERNAL or BASIC image.

args.name: highScoreFilenames
args.comment: Two overlapping filenames: $C100 is @:ATTACK MUTANT.HI (18 chars, used by SAVE), $C102 is ATTACK MUTANT.HI (16 chars, used by LOAD). The load name is the save name with the @: prefix skipped - one string serving both calls.

args.name: highScoreNamePad
args.comment: Ten $FF bytes then three zeros, immediately after the two filenames. Filler to the end of the loaded image at $C11F; nothing reads it.

args.text:
Self-modifying code: patches OPCODE bytes into seven sites in the $9C00-$9FFF routines, then runs them.

  #$C6 = DEC zp   -> $9C22, $9EEA, $9FBB
  #$99 = STA abs,Y -> $9E68
  #$9D = STA abs,X -> $9FB0
  #$DE = DEC abs,X -> $9EB8
  #$FE = INC abs,X -> $9C12

Every one of those is a WRITE or a decrement. $C046 is the exact mirror and pokes LDA in the same seven slots. So the code at $9DBB/$9E0A is one routine driven in two modes, and a static reading of those seven addresses is reading whichever opcode was poked last.

Evidence: byte-for-byte mirror pair, and marking $C046 a function decoded exactly the 10 instructions the byte reading predicted.

READ-mode half of the pair with $C023: pokes #$A5 (LDA zp) into $9C22/$9EEA/$9FBB, #$B9 (LDA abs,Y) into $9E68, #$BD (LDA abs,X) into $9C12/$9EB8/$9FB0, then falls through into $C061 which calls $9DBB.

Was sitting as data until marked a function; nothing references it absolutely, so it is reached by a computed or table dispatch that find_references cannot see.

CMP #$50 twice in a row, and the second is dead: if the first BEQ did not take, A is unchanged, so the second compare has the same result and its BEQ cannot take either. Reads as a leftover from an edit, probably two different key codes once. Live behaviour: $DC01 == $50 goes to $C012, anything else JMP $94AF.

Self-modifying patch: writes bytes into six sites in the sound and sprite code ($9C12, $9C22, $9E68, $9EB8, $9FB0, $9FBB) and then calls sub_9E0A. $C046 just below holds a second, unreferenced set of values for the same six addresses. Called from loc_9D59, which is on the $C000 path.

Not reached by any decode: 27 bytes with exactly the shape of sub_C023 above (LDA #$A5 / STA $9C22 / STA $9EEA / STA $9FBB / LDA #$B9 / STA $9E68 / LDA #$BD / STA $9C12 / STA $9EB8 / STA $9FB0). sub_C023 patches the same six addresses with a different set of values, so this is the other half of a pair - a second mode, or the undo - that nothing calls any more. Dead unless something reaches it through a computed jump.

Load the high score table from disk.
SETLFS 0,8,0 then SETNAM $10 chars at $C102 ("ATTACK MUTANT.HI"), then LOAD with A=0 (load) and X/Y = $5E00 as the destination, because secondary address 0 means "ignore the load address in the file header". So the table lives at $5E00, and the save at $C082 writes $5E00-$5ECF, which fixes its size at $D0 = 208 bytes.
Evidence: the filename bytes at $C102, and the $FB/$FC pointer set to $5E00 at $C0A5 with X/Y = $5ED0 at $C0AD before JSR SAVE.
Note the filename says ATTACK, not REVENGE. Either this build reuses the earlier game score file or the disk is mislabelled. Not resolved here.

Game over: write the high score table back to disk, then restart at $8A3C.
Does a full KERNAL I/O reset first (IOINIT / RESTOR / CINT, and CINV back to $EA31) because the game runs its own raster IRQ and has taken the machine over; SAVE needs the KERNAL IRQ and screen back. Border and background are blanked to 0 so the restored screen is not seen.
Saves $5E00-$5ECF under "@:ATTACK MUTANT.HI" - the @: prefix is the 1541 scratch-and-replace, so it overwrites rather than failing with FILE EXISTS.
Put the KERNAL back: IOINIT, RESTOR (which restores the $0314 vector table), CINT (screen editor init), then CINV = $EA31, the standard IRQ. Called only from the save path.

Take the machine over: raster IRQ in, NMI disabled, VIC into multicolour text.
- CINV = $88D5, the raster handler.
- NMINV = $88D4, which is a bare RTI. That is the standard way to make RESTORE do nothing.
- $0291 = $80 disables the Commodore+SHIFT charset toggle.
- $D01A = $81 enables the raster interrupt source; $D012 = $60 and $D011 bit 7 cleared put the split at raster line $60 (96).
- $D016: AND #$F7 clears CSEL (38-column, so the side borders open for smooth scrolling) and ORA #$10 sets MCM (multicolour text).
- $D418 = $0F, full volume.
Also seeds the music tempo: $10 = $11 = 7.

One byte, $40 = RTI, installed as the NMI vector at $0318. Pressing RESTORE therefore does nothing. It is also the byte immediately before the IRQ handler, so the two vectors are $88D4 and $88D5 - deliberate, not a coincidence.

Raster IRQ handler. If $D019 bit 0 is clear this was not the raster, so hand it to the KERNAL at $EA31 (the CIA timer IRQ is still running and still needs servicing). Otherwise bump the frame counter and go to the raster-split code at $8BC9.
Everything below - $88E4/$88EC/$88F7/$91BA - is the tail of that handler: it finishes by acknowledging $D019 and falling into $EA31 to restore registers and RTI.

Music player, voices 1 and 2, run once per raster interrupt. This and $91BA are three copies of one routine.
A tune is a stream of (ticks, note) byte pairs. The pointer is advanced by 2 BEFORE the read, which is why StartMusic seeds it two below the data: $13/$14 = $5FFE so the first pair read is at $6000.
Per voice: decrement the tick counter; when it hits zero, gate the voice off (STY $D404 with Y=0), step the pointer, read ticks into $17/$19/$2D and the note into A.
  note $F0 - a rest. Leave the voice gated off for this many ticks.
  note $FF - end of tune. Clears $1A so nothing plays until StartMusic is called again. (Voice 1 has no $FF test, only voices 2 and 3 do, so voice 1 relies on the others to stop the tune.)
  anything else - index into noteFreqLo/noteFreqHi at $898C/$89CD (65 notes) and gate on with $21 = triangle + gate.
$5F non-zero suppresses the gate-on in all three voices while leaving the frequency writes, which is how the tune is silenced without losing its place.
$10/$11 is a tempo divider: the whole player only runs every $11 interrupts.

Note frequency tables, 65 entries each: low bytes at $898C-$89CC, high bytes at $89CD-$8A0D. Indexed by the note byte in a tune, so a note is 0..64. The high bytes run 02..54, which is the usual five-and-a-bit octave equal-tempered table for a PAL SID.

The three letters T W O. sub_8A42 copies them over offsets 9-11 of the player two status line, turning the copied template PLAYER ONE into PLAYER TWO. Note the loop runs X = 3,2,1 and stops before X = 0, so $8A38 is never read - the string is $8A39, not $8A38.
"OF THE MUTANT CAMELS", 20 characters. Read by sub_9019 at $907E. The rest of the title is elsewhere - this is only the second line.

The 40-column status line, copied verbatim into both players lines at $5F00 and $5F80 by sub_8A42, which ANDs each byte with #$3F to turn PETSCII upper case into screen codes.
  "  PLAYER ONE  0000000  NEXT ZONE 00 KM  "
That fixes the field offsets used everywhere else: score is the seven digits at offset 14, the zone distance is the two digits at offset 33, and the word ONE is at offsets 9-11. sub_8A42 overwrites those three bytes of the SECOND copy with "TWO" from $8A39, which is the whole of what makes $5F80 the player two line.

The other 40-column panel line: "  NEUTRONIUM STATUS  HHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH ". The 18 H characters are the neutronium bar, and $915E holds exactly 18 colour bytes for them (07 07 07 04 04 04 repeated - yellow/purple in threes), which is what identifies the bar as 18 segments rather than a word.

Start the tune. Returns immediately if $1A says one is already playing.
Sets the three voice pointers two bytes below their data, because the player adds 2 before reading:
  voice 1  $13/$14 = $5FFE  ->  tune at $6000
  voice 2  $15/$16 = $631E  ->  tune at $6320
  voice 3  $2B/$2C = $659E  ->  tune at $65A0
The round destinations are what make this readable; the seeds themselves are not addresses of anything.
ADSR: attack/decay $0A on voices 1 and 2, $0C on voice 3, sustain/release 0 on all three - a plucked note with no sustain. Filter off, volume $0F. All three tick counters start at 1 so the first note is fetched on the very next interrupt.

CORRECTED (basalt): this copies a SPRITE SET, not a character set, and beryl reached the same conclusion independently. I have renamed it CopySpriteSet.

The caller puts an even index in $02. spriteSetSourceTable ($502F) is two interleaved byte tables read as LDA $502F,X (low) / LDA $5030,X (high), so X = 0,2,4,6,8,10 selects source $1000, $1800, $4000, $4800, $5000, $5800. It copies 2048 bytes to $0800-$0FFF ($05 is stepped until it reaches $10, which is what bounds it).

Evidence it is sprites:
- 2048 bytes at $0800 is 32 sprites of 64, i.e. VIC sprite pointer values $20-$3F.
- I rendered $1000 and $1800 through run_decoder as 24x21 monochrome sprites and got recognisable creatures at both. $4000 gives dithered multicolour-looking shapes. Not glyphs.
- The only write to VMCSB in the whole program is $8AE7 STA #$18, which puts the character base at $2000 and leaves it there; AnimateCharacters ($9206) writes character data to $2110 and $2148, confirming $2000. So $0800 is not the charset.
- Its caller $9CB5 sets SPMC0, SPMC1, XXPAND and YXPAND in the same breath.
- No instruction anywhere reads or writes $0800-$0FFF absolutely, which is what you expect of data only the VIC looks at.

NOTE this routine reuses $02-$05 as two pointers (source $02/$03, destination $04/$05), not as the PrintCharAt arguments those bytes hold everywhere else in this block.

Still unexplained: the last two table entries are $5000 and $5800, which is this program code. Either those slots are never selected, or the interleaved lo/hi reading is wrong for them.

"BEASTS REMAINING: n" on messageLine ($0590, screen row 10).
The digit is written at $05AD as '0' + beastsRemaining ($54). If the sum is still '0' - i.e. no beasts left - it calls ShowBeastsExtinct ($53EC) which overwrites the line with "YOUR BEASTS ARE EXTINCT, PLAYER ONE" ("TWO" patched in at $05B2 when playerState is 2). So $54 is the life count and this is the between-lives screen.

THE OPTIONS SCREEN. Reached from CheckOptionsKey ($52EE), which fires on LSTX $26 = the 'O' key.

Draws, via PrintCharAt ($883A):
  row 3 col 15  "OPTIONS"
  row 6 col 9   "WAVE SEQUENCY: NORMAL"   ($52E8 "RANDOM" overwrites col 24 when waveSequencyRandom is set)
  row 8 col 14  "PLAYERS: 1"              ('2' written at col 23 when playerState is non-zero)
  ShowZoneDistance ($5300) adds row 10 col 8 "DISTANCE BETWEEN ZONES: nn"

Then polls LSTX. The four codes it tests are the function keys in the C64 keyboard matrix:
  $04 = F1  toggle waveSequencyRandom ($59, EOR #$FF)
  $05 = F3  playerState ($56) = (playerState+1) AND 1  -> 1 or 2 players
  $06 = F5  zoneDistance ($57) += 2, wrapping $15 back to 7
  $03 = F7  leave: PLA/PLA to drop the caller's return address, JMP $8AEA

The PLA/PLA at $52B6 means this never returns to whoever called it - it exits straight into the game at $8AEA.

SWAP PLAYERS. playerState ($56) is a three-value thing, and this is where that shows:
  0 = one-player game
  1 = two-player game, player one up
  2 = two-player game, player two up

$56 = 0 -> save and restore the same slot, so the swap is a no-op.
$56 = 1 -> becomes 2, then falls into the save-to-slot-1 path.
$56 = 2 -> becomes 1, saves to slot 2.

A slot is 40 bytes of the status line ($5F00 for player one, $5F80 for player two) plus three bytes of per-player state: $58, $50 and beastsRemaining ($54), kept at $5F30-$5F32 and $5FB0-$5FB2. LoadPlayerStatusLine ($5359) is the other half.

The options screen toggles $56 between 0 and 1 only; the value 2 is only ever produced here.

Rebuild highScoreTable ($5E00) from defaultHighScoreTable ($5474) - the fallback when the .HI file did not load.
Fills $5E00-$5EFF with spaces, then copies $D0 = 208 bytes of ASCII masked AND #$3F.

highScoreTable ($5E00) is 4 entries of $34 = 52 bytes. Entry n starts at $5E00 + n*$34. Byte 0 is the rank digit '1'..'4'; bytes 1..7 are the 7 score digits; the rest is the name text. That layout is confirmed three ways: the $34 stride here, InitDefaultHighScores ($545C) copying $D0 = 4*$34 bytes, and the renumbering loop at $567F which writes '1'..'4' at $5E00, $5E34, $5E68, $5E9C.

The comparison walks Y = 1..7 comparing scoreField+Y ($040E-$0414, the score on the status line) against ($60),Y for each of the four entries in turn. Higher than an entry -> $556E inserts: the table below is shifted down $34 bytes ($5587 copies backwards until it hits a $FF sentinel), the new score is written in, and name entry begins at $55AE.

The table is loaded from disk at $C065 and saved back at $C082 (amber's finding); InitDefaultHighScores supplies it when the file is not there.

Block until a key is pressed, then return its game character code.
Waits for LSTX ($C5) to leave $40 (= no key), then translates through keyMatrixCodeTable/keyResultTable. An unrecognised key is ignored and the wait restarts. Returns $00 for INS/DEL (backspace) and $FF for RETURN.

KEY DECODE TABLES, and the proof that this game uses a CUSTOM CHARACTER SET.

ReadKeyMapped ($5695) searches keyMatrixCodeTable ($56CD) for the value in LSTX ($C5) and returns the byte at the same index in keyResultTable ($56AE). Lining the two tables up against the standard C64 keyboard matrix scan codes gives an exact, unambiguous mapping:

  index  result  matrix code  key
      0    $00        $00     INS/DEL   (handled as backspace at $5645)
      1    $01        $0A     A
      2    $02        $1C     B
    ...   ...        ...      ... straight through to
     26    $1A        $0C     Z
     27    $20        $3C     SPACE
     28    $51        $2C     . (full stop)
     29    $52        $2F     , (comma)
     30    $FF        $01     RETURN     (terminates name entry, $5659)

Every one of the 26 letters lines up. That pins two glyphs of the game's own charset:
  $51 = '.'   $52 = ','
which are NOT the standard screen codes ($2E and $2C). Two more follow from context in the message text:
  $54 = '!'   ($57A7 "WELL DONE! ... CAMELKIND!")
  $56 = ':'   ($52C9 "WAVE SEQUENCY: NORMAL", $52DE "PLAYERS: 1", $533F "DISTANCE BETWEEN ZONES: 00")

So the built-in screen/petscii decoders are correct for A-Z and space in this project and WRONG for punctuation. The charset itself is one of the blocks CopyCharSetToRAM ($5007) moves to $0800.

Draws "CHEAT MODE OPERATIVE" on messageLine when cheatFlag ($5E) is set, and sets $4F = 7.
Like the other ASCII-stored strings in this block ($5474, $57EF, $5848, $90F8) the text is held as plain uppercase ASCII/PETSCII and converted to screen codes at draw time with AND #$3F. The screen-code strings ($511B, $5199, $52C2...) are stored already converted. Both kinds are in this one block, which is worth knowing before declaring an encoding.

PAUSE. Any key down (LSTX not $40) puts "PAUSE" on messageLine and holds until the key is released and another is pressed. Returns immediately when cheatFlag ($5E) is set, so cheat mode disables pause.

basalt: note from outside this block, because it explains something in mine.

This reads a stream of parameter bytes through sub_9CFB (LDA ($3E),Y / INY) and distributes them: $53, $52, $51, $42, then $02, then SPMC0, SPMC1, one more byte, then 40 characters into messageLine-1 ($058F), then JSR CopyCharSetToRAM ($5007).

The six slots in that table are $1000, $1800, $4000, $4800, $5000, $5800 - the last two of which are program code, so either they are never selected or my reading of the interleaved lo/hi table is wrong. Whoever owns $3E/$3F can settle it by reading the descriptor data.

OBJECT SYSTEM. Two different things live in $1D00-$1FFF and they are indexed differently.

TYPE-INDEXED (Y = 0..7, one entry per creature type in this wave):
  $1D00 typeSpawnTimer  counts down; at zero sub_9744 spawns one of that type
  $1DA0-$1E37          the WAVE DESCRIPTOR, 152 bytes = 19 tables of 8, copied
                       wholesale from the level stream by loc_9699 (CPY #$98)

SLOT-INDEXED (X = object slot, 16 wide):
  $1D10 objType   which template this slot was made from (sub_9772 $97BF: TYA STA $1D10,X)
  $1D20..$1D90, $1E40, $1E50, $1E70, $1E80, $1E90, $1FB0

sub_9772 is the spawn: it copies one column of the template block into the matching slot arrays. That mapping is what named these:

  tmplShape     $1DB0 -> objShape    $1D30  and sprShape $1F70
  tmplField40   $1DB8 -> objField40  $1D40
  tmplField50   $1DC0 -> objField50  $1D50, and AND #$3F -> objAnimBase $1D20
  tmplSpeedX    $1DE0 -> objSpeedX   $1D60  and objBaseSpeedX $1E70
  tmplSpeedY    $1DE8 -> objSpeedY   $1D70  and objBaseSpeedY $1E80
  tmplField80   $1DF0 -> objField80  $1D80
  tmplSpawnLimit$1DF8 -> objSpawnLimit $1D90
  tmplColour    $1E18 -> sprColour   $1F60
  tmplFieldE90  $1E20 -> objFieldE90 $1E90

$1DF8 bit 7 means the type is capped: $9764 masks the low nibble and compares it with $4D, refusing the spawn once that many exist.

loc_96B0 seeds $1D00-$1D07 from $1DA0-$1DA7 and then zeroes $1D08-$1D9F, which is the whole slot space, at wave start.

The field names ending in a bare address are honest: the copy proves they are one field, the meaning is not settled.

objXPos / objYPos, and SLOT 0 IS THE PLAYER.

loc_5049 reads objXPos,X, compares it with objXPos (element 0) and then sets bit 7 of objBaseSpeedX,X when the object is at or beyond the player and clears it when it is not, mirroring the result into objSpeedX,X. loc_506A does the same for Y through objBaseSpeedY / objSpeedY.

That is homing: bit 7 of the speed byte is its sign, and the creature is turned to face slot 0. It only makes sense if slot 0 is the thing being chased.

Corroboration: ShowBeastsRemaining ($50DE) plants #$C0 into objXPos before drawing the status line, and $95B9 / loc_962E move objXPos+1 and objYPos+1 with INC and DEC, i.e. slot 1 under some other control.

What I have NOT established: whether slot 0 is the player ship or the camel being defended. The game is about defending camels, so either reading is live.

SPRITE MULTIPLEXER STATE. Sixteen virtual sprites on eight hardware ones, alternated frame by frame.

loc_925F toggles $30 between 0 and 1 every frame and then, for hardware sprite X = 8..1, renders EITHER virtual sprite X-1 (arrays $1F40-$1F47 etc.) on even frames OR virtual sprite X+7 (arrays $1F48-$1F4F etc.) on odd frames. sub_929D does the first, sub_92CF the second; both write SP0X+2*(X-1) and SP0Y+2*(X-1).

So every array here is 16 entries: 0-7 are the frame-0 half and 8-15 the frame-1 half.

  $1F40  sprX      X position
  $1F50  sprY      Y position
  $1F60  sprColour SPMC1 value; bit 7 means auto-increment it every frame (sub_929D $92B7), i.e. colour-cycle
  $1F70  sprShape  sprite pointer, written straight to $07F8+n
  $1F80  sprInUse  0 = free. sub_92F6 allocates (writes $88), sub_9328 frees.

$1F98/$1F99 are the two $D015 enable masks and $1F9C/$1F9D the two $D010 MSB-of-X masks, one per frame parity. sub_92F6 ORs the new sprite's bit into $1F98 when the slot is 0-7 and into $1F99 when it is 8-15 (it tests bit 3 of the slot number).

Evidence: $92CB STA $07F7,X with X=1..8 writes $07F8-$07FF, which pins the screen at $0400 and the sprite pointers where the hardware expects them.

ASSEMBLER SOURCE LEFT IN THE SHIPPED BINARY. Not data the game uses - residue from the machine it was built on, saved into the image because this range was never cleared.

It is stored the way a Commodore assembler that lives inside BASIC stores it: a chain of [link lo][link hi][line number lo][line number hi] text $00. Following the links from $5877 gives line numbers 13880 to 13990 in steps of ten, which is what proves the format rather than a coincidence of printable bytes:

  13880   STA $07F7,X
  13890   RTS
  13900  SSET TYA
  13910   PHA
  13920   AND #$07
  13930   SEC
  13940   TAY
  13950   INY
  13960   LDA #$00
  13970  TANGE ROL A
  13980   DEY
  13990   BNE TANGE (the operand runs off the end of the salvaged text)

SSET/TANGE is a bit-mask builder: take a sprite number 0-7, shift a 1 left that many places. STA $07F7,X with X = 1..8 writes $07F8-$07FF, the sprite shape pointers for a screen at $0400 - which is where this game puts the screen. So these eleven lines are a sprite-enable and shape-set routine from the original source, and the author called the mask loop TANGE and its entry SSET.

The chain breaks at $5906 because the next link points at $3202, outside this block. There are two more fragments at $5F28 and $5FA8.

More assembler source residue, same [link][line number]text$00 format as $5870. Lines 15150-15200:

  15150   CLC
  15160   ADC #$C8
  15170   STA NEXINI
  15180   LDA NEXINI+1
  15190   ADC #$00

Adding 200 to a 16-bit pointer the author called NEXINI, and 200 is the size of the on-screen play area in rows or the stride of a table. The plain text just above at $5F26 reads "   LDA NEX", the tail of the line before this fragment.

These bytes are overwritten at runtime: $5F00-$5F27 is the player one status line, so the game writes over the start of this block on the first frame. It survives in the image only because it was in memory when the build was saved.

The third and best fragment of leftover assembler source. Lines 15240-15260:

  15240  MLOOP JSR STARF
  15250        JSR BULITZ
  15260        JSR CCAMEL

That is the game main loop in the author own names: STARF is the starfield, BULITZ the bullets, CCAMEL the camels. Just above, at $5FA6 and $5FB3, are the tails of two more lines: "  ONZER JM" and "NI1 ; READ DATA TABLE" - so there is a label ONZER (zone-related) and a commented-out READ DATA TABLE.

A caution about using these: they are names from SOME build, not necessarily this one, and the fragments are eight lines out of a program of thousands. They are evidence about intent, not an index. Nothing here has been renamed on their authority.

ZONE DATA TABLE. 42 records of 200 ($C8) bytes, $6700-$87CF, immediately below the code at $87FE with 46 bytes of slack.

The arithmetic that identifies it is at $93D8: $3E/$3F is loaded with $6700 and then $C8 is added once per zone, X coming from zoneNumber ($58). $9699 then copies $98 = 152 bytes from ($3E),Y into $1DA0, so 152 of each 200-byte record are used and 48 are slack.

The record count is fixed by $9DA0: after a zone, $58 is incremented and compared with #$2A, so zones run 0 to 41 - 42 of them, 42 x 200 = 8400 = $20D0 bytes, $6700 + $20D0 = $87D0. The table ends exactly where the data does.

The 152 bytes are 19 groups of 8: one row per attribute, one column per object type, since the game has 8 object types per zone. The destination labels give the layout - $1DA0 spawn interval, $1DA8, $1DB0 shape, $1DB8, $1DC0, ... $1DE0 speed X, $1DE8 speed Y, $1DF0, $1DF8 spawn limit, $1E00, $1E10, $1E18 colour, $1E20.

So a zone is not a map: it is a table of what may spawn, how often, how fast, what shape and what colour. That is the whole level design of this game.

Copy this zone template block into the working tables: 152 bytes from ($3E),Y - which StartZone has pointed at $6700 + 200*zoneNumber - into $1DA0 upwards. Every tmpl* array is a slice of this one copy.

ZONE COMPLETE. Silences all three SID voices, waits for every active sprite to walk off screen (the loop at $9D6E pushes each objXPos up until it wraps and then frees the sprite), then advances the zone.

$9D9C-$9DB3 is where the game length is decided: INC zoneNumber, and if it reaches #$2A = 42 the player has finished all 42 zones - show WELL DONE, bump loopNumber ($50), cap it at 5, and set the zone back to 0 so the game loops harder. That is the only place either counter changes, so 42 zones per loop and 6 loops of difficulty is the whole progression.

Note $9DB5: LDX #$F8 / TXS resets the stack pointer before jumping to $937B, so this never returns to whoever called it. Anything reasoning about the call graph through here is wrong.

Set the VIC per-sprite flag bits for one object type. X is the sprite number, Y the object type.

Builds 1<<(X AND 7) into printColour ($05) and 1<<Y into $06, then tests $06 against three per-type masks - $53 multicolour, $51 X-expand, $52 Y-expand - and ORs the sprite bit into $D01C, $D01D and $D017 respectively. So the zone data says which object TYPES are multicoloured or expanded, and this turns that into the per-SPRITE register bits at the moment a sprite is allocated.

Worth comparing with the leftover source at $5870, which contains the same idea written differently:
  SSET TYA / PHA / AND #$07 / SEC / TAY / INY / LDA #$00 / TANGE ROL A / DEY / BNE TANGE
That version uses SEC+ROL and this one CLC+ASL, so it is a rewrite rather than the same code - but SSET is what the author called this.

Two more glyphs, found later in the wave banners at $6700 and the scroll text at $5A00:

  $55 = question mark ("WHAT IS A BRAHM, ANYWAY?", "MORE TEA, VICAR?")

NOT GAME DATA. This is leftover text from the machine the game was written on: 6502 source lines held in BASIC line format - 2-byte link, 2-byte line number, then the text, then $00.    TANGE ROL A / DEY / BNE ...

More of the same is at $5F26-$5FFF, underneath the player status save slots, and that fragment carries the author's own routine names:

   ONZER JM... / NI1 ; READ DATA TABLE
   MLOOP JSR STARF / JSR BULITZ / JSR CCAMEL

So the main loop was called MLOOP and it called STARF, BULITZ and CCAMEL - starfield, bullets and camel. ADC #$C8 next to NEXINI is the same $C8 stride as the wave table at $6700, which is a second, independent confirmation of that record size.

THE ATTACK WAVE TABLE. 42 records of 200 ($C8) bytes: $6700 to $87CF. This is the single largest thing in the program and nothing referred to it absolutely, so it was invisible to find_references.

How the base and stride were established, at $93AB:
  93D8  LDA #$67 / STA $3F      zoneDataPtr high = $67
  93DC  LDA #$00 / STA $3E      zoneDataPtr low  = $00
  93E0  LDX $58 (zoneNumber); loop: zoneDataPtr += $C8, DEX
So record n is at $6700 + n*200 and everything in a wave is read through ($3E),Y by sub_9CFB.

Within a record, bytes $A0-$C7 are the 40-character banner shown when the wave starts. That offset is fixed: every one of the 42 lands exactly on a record boundary + $A0, which is what makes the whole layout provable rather than guessed. Bytes $00-$9F are the wave parameters, distributed by $9CB5 and its callers (sprite multicolours, expand flags, a character set index into charSetSourceTable, and more I did not chase).

42 is confirmed independently by the game's own credits text at $5A00: "THE GAME CONSISTS OF FORTY TWO DIFFERENT ATTACK WAVES". The last record $8708-$87CF ends 46 bytes before code resumes at $87FE.

THE RANDOM NUMBER GENERATOR, and it does not read RAM.

  INC $24 / LDX $24 / LDA $A000,X / RTS

$A000-$BFFF in this image is 8192 bytes of ZERO — I checked every page. If this read RAM the generator would return 0 forever and eleven callers would all take the same branch every time.

It does not read RAM. Nothing in this program writes $00 or $01 (I searched: zero instructions touch the processor port), so the 6510 port keeps its power-on $37 and BASIC ROM is banked in over $A000-$BFFF. This reads a byte of BASIC ROM and calls it a random number.

That is a well-worn C64 trick and it is why the game needs no seed and no arithmetic: the ROM is a fixed 8K block of high-entropy-looking bytes that is always there. It is also perfectly deterministic — the same $24 gives the same byte on every machine and every run — which is the sort of thing that matters if anyone ever tries to reproduce a wave.

Eleven callers: $8CD4, $8CE1, $8D6F, $8DAC, $8EB9, $8F31, $8F3A, $9387, $97EF, $9804, $9858. TitleColourAndSoundStep at $50BD reads the same table directly, taking AND #$03 of it to pick a border colour.

re64 cannot see any of this: the memory model is flat and a project layer supplying $A000 wins over a ROM nobody has loaded. The zeros are real bytes of the runtime image; they are just never what the CPU reads.

Read as six-byte rows they draw a hillside, top of the column first:

  20 20 20 20 26 28      . . . . / #
  20 20 20 26 28 28      . . . / # #
  20 20 20 27 28 28      . . . \ # #
  20 20 20 20 27 28      . . . . \ #
  20 20 20 20 20 27      . . . . . \

$20 is blank, $28 is solid ground, and $26 and $27 are the rising and falling slope glyphs of the game font. Loop over the frames and you get a hill that climbs and comes back down.

Write one object position into the sprite shadow registers, and maintain the X most-significant-bit mask.

X is the object slot. Sprite index is (X AND 7) so slots 0-7 and 8-15 share the eight hardware sprites - this game multiplexes two sets of eight over the raster split. $07 is the X coordinate in character-ish units and is doubled, $08 the Y. They go to sprX $1F40 and sprY $1F50.

The carry out of ASL is the ninth X bit, and it is folded into sprMsbXMaskFrame0 $1F9C or $1F9D depending on bit 3 of the slot number - one mask per half of the multiplex. Clearing goes through EOR #$FF / AND and setting through ORA, which is why the two halves of this routine look duplicated: they are the same shift with opposite bit operations.

RASTER PHASE DISPATCH. $1E is not really a frame counter, it is a phase counter 0-1-2, bumped by the IRQ at $88DF, and this picks which of three raster splits has just fired:

  phase 1  -> next raster $D8, and $D016 X-scroll bits set from scrollX ($1F)
  phase 2  -> next raster $F8, X-scroll bits cleared and $D011 bit 7 cleared
  phase 0  -> next raster $90; this is the one that does the work

So the play field scrolls smoothly between rasters $D8 and $F8 and the panel above it does not, which is the classic split-scroll.

The work phase reads $D01E (sprite/sprite collision) into $44 - reading it clears it, so this is the only place collisions are latched - then runs the key check, the title flash, object movement every other frame ($20), and the horizontal scroll.

SCROLLING: DEC $1F each pass. At 4 it calls AnimateCharacters. When it passes $FF it reloads 7 and shifts whole character columns left by one, the loop at $8C53 copying $0630 to $062F and so on. Fine scroll for seven steps, coarse scroll on the eighth - textbook, and it means the play field is character-mapped, not bitmapped.

CCAMEL - control the camel. Joystick port 2 at $DC00, bits active LOW: $01 up, $02 down, $04 left, $08 right, $10 fire.

The camel is object slot 0: objXPos, objYPos, objFieldFB0 and sprShape all at index 0. Bit 7 of objFieldFB0 is the facing flag.

Runs on a divider - DEC camelTick ($34), and only acts when it reaches zero, reloading $80. So the camel moves once every 128 ticks of whatever drives the main loop, which is what makes it walk rather than fly.

Ground behaviour:
  right  -> INC objXPos, clamped at $90
  left   -> face left (objFieldFB0 = $80, shape $C0), refused at objXPos $11
  up     -> jump: camelMode = 1, jumpVelocity = $0F, jumpHeldRight remembers whether right was also held, shape $CD
  down   -> camelMode = 2, shape $CE, refused at the left limit
Neither left nor right, or the right limit reached, falls into $9492 which clears the facing flag and JMPs to $C000 - the keyboard check.

camelMode ($33) is the state machine: 0 walking, 1 rising, 2 ducking, 5 landing. Non-zero sends this routine to the physics at $94F6 instead of reading the stick, so you cannot steer while airborne except by the direction you were already holding.

Jump physics, reached when camelMode is not zero.

Mode 1, rising and falling: objYPos changes by jumpVelocity ($39), treated as SIGNED - bit 7 set means add the complement instead of subtracting, which is how the same counter serves both halves of the arc. jumpVelocity is decremented every step, so it counts $0F, $0E ... $00, $FF ... down to $F0, giving a symmetric parabola sixteen steps up and sixteen down. At $F0 the camel has landed: camelMode becomes 5, and voice 3 gets a short $0300 triangle burst with attack/decay $0C - the thud.

If jumpHeldRight was set the camel keeps drifting right for the whole jump, clamped at $90 like on the ground.

BULITZ - the bullet. There is exactly ONE, object slot 1, and $3B bulletDirection is both the flag that it exists and the direction it travels.

Firing: on a $0C-tick repeat delay ($3C). Requires fire down AND at least one direction down - the CMP #$0F test rejects fire with the stick centred, so this game has no straight-ahead shot, only eight-way. The direction bits are saved whole into $3B and the bullet then moves by them for its whole life; you cannot steer it.

It also refuses to fire unless camelMode is 0, 1 or 5 - so you can shoot while running, rising or landing, but not while ducking (mode 2).

The bullet starts at the camel position plus ($13, $02) and moves 2 pixels vertically or 1 horizontally per step, which makes diagonals steeper than 45 degrees.

It dies at $9677 when it reaches X $06 or $B0, or Y $10, $0F, $F8 or $F9. Two pairs of Y limits because the vertical step is 2 and the counter can pass a limit on either parity - checking one value would let a bullet escape half the time. That is a real detail, not redundancy.

Sound: a falling-pitch pulse on voice 1, but only if no tune is playing ($1A) - so in-game the laser and the music share voice 1 and the music wins.

The laser sound decay. Reuses voice1NoteTicks ($17) as the pitch: decrement it, write it straight to $D401 as the frequency high byte, and gate the voice off when it reaches zero. So the shot is a downward sweep from $40 to $00 over 64 calls. $3D is the flag that this is running.

Worth noting because it is why the music player and the shot fight over voice 1: they use the same zero page byte for two different purposes.

MOVEMENT HANDLER 1: constant speed, expressed as a COUNTDOWN rather than a rate.

X and Y are handled identically. Take objSpeedX,X; if it is zero do nothing. Otherwise split it into a sign (bit 7) and a magnitude (bits 0-6), decrement the magnitude, and put it back with the sign restored. When the magnitude reaches zero, reload it from objBaseSpeedX,X and move objXPos,X by objField80,X — adding when bit 7 of the reload value is clear, subtracting when it is set.

So the byte is a delay, not a velocity: a LARGER value means a SLOWER object. objBaseSpeedX / objBaseSpeedY hold the reload and the direction, and objField80 is the step in pixels.

That is what makes loc_5049 work. It sets or clears bit 7 of objBaseSpeedX,X and objBaseSpeedY,X by comparing this object against slot 0, which is the player — one bit each, and the creature turns to face you.

MOVEMENT HANDLER 2: ballistic, and it reads the SAME fields differently. Worth knowing before naming anything in the object arrays: there is no single meaning for objSpeedX.

Horizontal: the LOW NIBBLE of objSpeedX,X is a step in pixels, applied every frame, added or subtracted on bit 7. No countdown.

Vertical: objSpeedY,X is a signed velocity that is DECREMENTED every frame, which is gravity. While it is positive the object rises by that much; once bit 7 is set the object falls, one pixel at a time, up to $FF-value steps.

The fall stops at objYPos = $E0, the ground line, and then one of three things happens on objField80,X:
  zero          -> objSpeedY = #$10, a fixed bounce
  bit 7 set     -> $9A29 mixes sub_9856 with objField80, masks to 7 bits and adds 4, a varying bounce
  otherwise     -> DEC objField80,X, then LDY objField80,X and JMP sub_9772, which RESPAWNS THIS SLOT as a different template. So objField80 is a countdown of bounces, and when it runs out the thing turns into something else.

That last branch is the most interesting thing in the object system: a creature can metamorphose on landing.

THE ANIMATION STEPPER, and it names four object fields at once.

  objAnimFirst $1D30  first frame
  objAnimLast  $1D40  the frame to stop or turn at
  objAnimMode  $1D50  bit 6 = ping-pong, bit 7 = currently running backwards, low 6 bits = the frame delay
  objAnimDelay $1D20  the countdown, reloaded from tmplAnimMode AND #$3F

sprShape,X is the live frame — the same byte the multiplexer writes into $07F8+n, so animating an object is literally counting its sprite pointer up.

Three behaviours:
- objAnimFirst equals objAnimLast: nothing moves, a still sprite.
- bit 6 clear: INC sprShape until it reaches objAnimLast, then snap back to objAnimFirst. A loop.
- bit 6 set: INC to objAnimLast, then set bit 7 and DEC back to objAnimFirst, then clear it. A ping-pong.

UpdateOneObject at $9910 is the per-object tick: count objAnimDelay down, animate, move by type, age, draw.

OBJECT LIFETIME, and this is the metamorphosis mechanic.

objLifetime,X counts down every tick. At zero it is reloaded from tmplLifetime,Y and the object CHANGES INTO SOMETHING ELSE: $9A4F reads $1DD8,Y — the ninth template table, which renders here as spriteSet1 + $05D8 only because the label at $1800 carries a 2K extent that reaches this far — and

  $FF        -> sub_9328, free the slot. The thing dies.
  anything else -> sub_9772 with that as the new type. The thing becomes it.

So $1DD8 is tmplNextType and the creature templates form a CHAIN: each type says what it turns into and how long it has first. Together with the bounce-countdown respawn at $9A20 that is two independent routes from one creature to another, and it is the mechanic that makes a Minter attack wave keep changing shape while you watch.

THE CHEAT CODE, and it spells GOATS.

cheatKeySequence ($96F7) is five keyboard matrix scan codes: $1A $26 $0A $16 $0D = G, O, A, T, S. The routine reads them as two overlapping tables, which is why the data looks one byte short of what the code implies:

  CMP cheatKeySequence,X     ($96F7 + progress) - the key already accepted: still held, do nothing
  CMP cheatKeySequence+1,X   ($96F8 + progress) - the next key wanted: accept it, INC cheatProgress
  anything else              - cheatProgress = 0, start again

cheatProgress ($5F) runs 0-4 and when it reaches 4 the accumulator still holds 4, so STA cheatFlag ($5E) sets cheat mode to a non-zero value and jumps to $9406. From there ShowCheatModeBanner ($57D1) puts "CHEAT MODE OPERATIVE" on the message line and CheckPauseKey ($5817) returns without pausing.

The letters were decoded against the standard C64 keyboard matrix, the same table that proves the game charset at $56AE: 26=G, 38=O, 10=A, 22=T, 13=S. Five for five, in that order, in a Jeff Minter game about camels.

(basalt, writing inside amber block - say the word and I will leave the naming to you.)

SCORING. Y is the object type, and the points come from tmplScoreValue at $1E28 - one byte per type, part of the zone record, so the same creature is worth different amounts in different zones.

The byte is packed: low nibble = which score digit, high nibble = how many times to add one to it. scoreField is $040D and the seven digits are $040E-$0414, so digit 7 is units, 6 is tens, 5 is hundreds. $15 is therefore one hundred, $56 is fifty, $55 is five hundred. Carry is propagated by hand at $9BCD: a digit passing $3A wraps to $30 and the loop moves one place left.

The score is kept in ASCII digits in screen memory and nowhere else - there is no binary copy anywhere. Same design as the neutronium bar.

It also fires the hit sound: voice 2 gated on with attack/decay $0A, and $41 set to 4 so $9B6D sweeps it. A score value of 0 or $FF scores nothing and makes no noise, which is how a zone marks a creature as harmless or as scenery.

Explosion. tmplExplodeLength at $1E30 - again per type, per zone - gives the number of DrainNeutronium calls the explosion runs for, so an explosion COSTS FUEL. Then voice 3 is gated with frequency high $08 for the bang.

It borrows printColour ($05) as the loop counter and printChar ($04) to save X, which is why this routine appears to touch the print variables without printing anything.

Drain one step of neutronium.

INC the current bar cell; when it reaches $50 the segment is used up, so blank it to $20 and DEC neutroniumLeft. The two instructions that do that, at $9C12 and $9C22, are the ones $C023 and $C046 rewrite - see the comment there.

When neutroniumLeft reaches zero the camel is out of fuel, and which of two things happens depends on zoneOverFlag: $0F means this is the deliberate end-of-zone drain, so set it to $FF and let EmptyNeutroniumBar see that and stop; anything else means the player has run out during play, so titleFlashCounter goes to 1 and that is what starts the death sequence.

Every three drains ($4B) it steps $4C down through neutroniumColourRamp at $9C4A - 00 0C 0E 0C 0A 09 08 - into camelColourTarget ($40), which $9B6D then fades the camel sprite towards. So the camel visibly changes colour as its fuel runs down, and the ramp being read backwards is why the sequence looks reversed in the data.

END OF ZONE: empty the bar, then fill it again. This is the bonus sequence.

First half ($9E10): zoneOverFlag = $0F, then call DrainNeutronium over and over with a falling siren on voice 1 ($00 down to $C0 in the frequency high byte) until the flag turns $FF, which DrainNeutronium does when the last segment goes. printRow counts how many drains it took - that is the bonus.

Second half ($9E52 onwards): double that count, then refill the bar from cell 1 upward with a rising siren, using the self-modified instructions at $9E68 and $9EB8.

So the reward for finishing a zone with fuel left is measured by emptying the bar and counting, which is exactly the kind of thing you do when the bar is the only place the number is kept.

CORRECTION, with evidence: this is unreachable, and READ mode is never entered in this build.

- find_references reports no inbound reference.
- The two bytes $46 $C0 do not occur ANYWHERE in the 47K image, so no lo/hi pointer table and no pushed address can reach it either. Only arithmetic on a computed address could, and nothing here does that.
- The loaded image already holds the WRITE opcodes at all seven patched sites: $9C12 is $FE (INC abs,X), $9C22 is $C6 (DEC zp), $9E68 is $99 (STA abs,Y), $9EB8 is $DE (DEC abs,X). So the program starts in WRITE mode.

Which makes sub_C023 a re-assertion of the state the program already ships in, and this routine the half that would undo it and never runs. Read as a debug or development switch left in - the same shape as the dead CMP #$50 at $C007 that disables the start-at-zone-41 branch just below.

That matters for anyone reading $9C0C, $9E0A or $9F90: those routines only ever run in WRITE mode, so the opcodes the listing shows are the ones that execute.

Clear the 40-character message line ($058F-$05B6) to spaces, then TAIL-JUMP into ShowCheatModeBanner ($57D1) rather than return - so clearing the line immediately puts "CHEAT MODE OPERATIVE" back if cheatFlag is set. That is why ShowCheatModeBanner ends by setting messageTimer ($4F) = 7: the banner is a message like any other and re-arms its own countdown.

Eight callers, all of them "I have finished with the message line".

The message line countdown, called once per frame from CheckPauseKey ($5817).

messageTickDivider ($4E) counts $60 frames; on each expiry it ticks TickZoneDistance ($9D2C) and then, if messageTimer ($4F) is non-zero, decrements it and recolours the whole message line from messageColourCycle ($9D21) = black, blue, red, purple, green, cyan, yellow, white - indexed by the timer, so the line cycles through seven colours over about seven seconds. When the timer reaches zero it jumps to ClearMessageLine.

So every banner in the game - BEASTS REMAINING, STAND BY YOUR BEAST, CHEAT MODE OPERATIVE, the wave name - is written to $0590 and then colour-cycled and wiped by this one routine.

Count down "NEXT ZONE nn KM" on the status line. zoneKmTickDivider ($47) divides by $10; each expiry decrements the ones digit at $0422, borrowing into the tens at $0421 when it passes $2F (below screen-code 0), and when both reach 0 the zone is complete.

Refill the bar, second half of the end-of-zone sequence. StepBarCellDown at $9EB6 walks the current cell down from $4F towards $47; when it gets there the cell is full, so it steps to the next one and the camel colour walks back UP the ramp at $9C4A - the inverse of the drain. It stops either at cell $13 (bar full, and $9EEA pulls the index back) or when printRow, the doubled bonus count, runs out.

A rising siren on voice 1 runs alongside, $00 up to $40, which is exactly the falling siren of the drain played backwards.

Add to the score without going through a type. PHA PHA then JMP into the middle of AddScoreForType at $9BCB, which is the point after that routine has pushed Y and X - so the two dummy pushes exist only to balance the two pulls at $9BE4. X is the digit column and Y the number of ones to add.

Its one caller, $9E22, passes X = 6, Y = 3 on every step of the end-of-zone drain. Digit 6 is the tens column, so finishing a zone pays THIRTY POINTS per step of neutronium left. That is the entire end-of-level bonus, and this is where the number lives.

Move type 2: give this object the direction the player last fired in. bulletDirection ($3B) holds the raw joystick bits from the shot, and they become speed $81 (negative 1) or $01 in X and Y. Reached from the type dispatch at $9C9F.

So a zone can declare a creature that chases the direction of your last shot. That is not something a static table could express, which is presumably why it is a code case rather than a data field.

THE CAMEL DIES. Reached from $9465 when titleFlashCounter says the neutronium ran out.

The animation is three loops, each of them DelayXY-paced so it plays at a watchable speed regardless of what the raster is doing:
  $9F67  shape $CD, objYPos[0] counted DOWN to $80  - the camel rises off the top of the screen
  $9F7E  shape $9C, objYPos[0] counted UP to $C8    - it comes back down
  $9F90  objXPos[0] counted down to zero            - it walks off to the left
Every sprite but the camel is freed first ($9F53 over slots 1-7).

Then $9F9D: reset camelMode, the jump state and the move type, refill the neutronium bar to eighteen full cells, reset the colour ramp, and DEC beastsRemaining ($54). If any beast is left, show the count, swap players and start the zone again at $93AB. If not, this is game over: check the high score table and JMP $C082, which writes it to disk and restarts the game.

So a life costs one beast and always restarts the CURRENT zone with a full bar - there is no progress penalty beyond the beast.

FOUR SEPARATE ROUTES from one creature to another — shot, exploded, aged out, and bounced out ($9A20) — all landing in the same sub_9772. That is the whole design: a wave is a directed graph of eight creature types, and the zone record is its adjacency list.

Verified against real data. Wave 0 gives moveType all 1 or 2, animFirst/animLast all in $90-$EE which is sprite data inside residentSprites, nextType all 0-6 or $FF, colour all 0-15 with the odd bit 7. Nineteen columns of plausible values is not something a wrong stride produces.

THE PLAYER, and it is a camel — I drew it.

Sprite block $C0 lives at $C0*64 = $3000, and the player-control routine at $94AA writes #$C0 into sprShape (virtual sprite 0) when you press left, #$CD at $94CF for fire+up and #$CE at $94E5 for fire+down. Rendering those blocks gives a quadruped with a long neck and a head — a camel, in a standing frame and three leaping ones at $3340.

That closes three separate chains at once. The player is virtual sprite slot 0 and object slot 0, which is what loc_5049 compares every creature against when it turns them to face you. The shapes are in $2800-$3FFF, addressable by the VIC without copying, which is why the bank-swap table at $502F never mentions them. And it confirms the whole sprite-multiplexer reading, because sprShape really is the byte that ends up at $07F8.

TEXT SCROLLED INTO THE TERRAIN. Called from $8CAB once per new landscape column, and this is what puts the credits, the high score table and "HERE WE GO" into the scenery rather than onto a text line - which is why none of that text is drawn by PrintCharAt anywhere.

It fills the seven characters of the new column ($1FF0 newColumnChars) with spaces and then plants one or two characters into it.

attractScrollState ($5A) is a mode byte with a counter in the low nibble:
  $00        off - $8CA9 skips this routine entirely
  $01-$0F    attract mode. Column row 3 gets highScoreTable[scrollIndex] and row 5 gets
             attractScrollText[scrollIndex] through scrollTextPtr, colour 1 (white). scrollIndex
             ($5B) advances one per column; when it wraps past $FF the pointer high byte steps,
             and when that reaches $5E - the end of the credits text - attractScrollState is
             zeroed and the scroll stops.
  $10-$1F    "HERE WE GO" ($5756), one character per column, rows 3 and 5, colour 4. The low
             nibble indexes the string; INC then AND #$1F means after 16 columns it becomes $00
             and the routine switches itself off.

Set to $03 at $8AAF when the program starts (attract mode) and to $10 at $8FA6, immediately before ShowStandByYourBeast - so "HERE WE GO" scrolls past you as a life begins.

Two streams share one index: the high score table and the credits text are both walked by scrollIndex, so during attract the landscape carries both at once, on different rows.

COMMIT THE SPRITES. There is a two-bank frame multiplexer here and IT NEVER RUNS IN THIS BUILD. Both halves matter, so take them apart carefully.

The machinery: $30 toggles 0/1 every call. $D015 gets sprEnableMaskFrame0 masked by $32 ORed with the mask for the current phase, and $D010 the same for the X most-significant bits. Then for X = 8 down to 1 it looks at sprInUse[$1F87+X] - that is slots 8 to 15 - and draws hardware sprite X-1 from bank 0 via $929D or bank 1 via $92CF depending on whether that slot is occupied and which phase it is. Sixteen object slots, eight sprites, alternating frames.

Why it is inert: nothing ever occupies slots 8-15. SSET marks sprInUse[Y] and every caller passes Y in 0..7 - FindFreeObjectSlot only searches 2 to $42-1 and $42 is 8 in 41 of the 42 zones and 6 in the other. ClearObjectSlots at $8B20 writes $FF into sprInUse[0] and sprInUse[8] and zero everywhere else, and nothing clears or sets $1F89-$1F8F afterwards. So the test at $9283 finds zero for X = 2..8 and takes $929D every time, and $1F88 is $FF which $92CF refuses outright. Bank 1 - the shadow registers at $1F48/$1F58/$1F68/$1F78 - is written by nothing and read by nothing.

So the game shows eight sprites, always from slots 0-7, with no flicker. The multiplexer is either unfinished or was disabled by narrowing $42 to 8 in every zone. If a zone record ever carried $42 greater than 8 the second bank would light up, which makes that byte the switch.

(This corrects what I first wrote here, which said objects 8-15 flicker at 25Hz. The code says they would; the data says there are none.)

$92CB and $92F2 both write $07F8-$07FF, the sprite shape pointers, which independently confirms the screen is at $0400.

SSET - and that is the author own name, matched instruction for instruction against the leftover assembler source at $5870.

The source fragment reads:
  13880   STA $07F7,X
  13890   RTS
  13900  SSET TYA
  13910   PHA
  13920   AND #$07
  13930   SEC
  13940   TAY
  13950   INY
  13960   LDA #$00
  13970  TANGE ROL A
  13980   DEY
  13990   BNE TANGE

And the code here is $92F2 STA $07F7,X / $92F5 RTS / $92F6 TYA / PHA / AND #$07 / SEC / TAY / INY / LDA #$00 / $92FF ROL A / DEY / BNE $92FF. Every instruction, in order, including the RTS and the STA of the routine before it. So $92CF is the routine those first two lines end, $92F6 is SSET and $92FF is TANGE.

That is the only place in this project where a name is taken from the source rather than inferred, and it is safe because the match is exact rather than thematic.

What it does: allocate a sprite for object slot Y. Build 1<<(Y AND 7), OR it into sprEnableMaskFrame0 or Frame1 depending on bit 3 of the slot - so slots 0-7 and 8-15 go to different halves of the multiplex - and mark sprInUse[Y] = $88. Slots 8-15 additionally flip their bit in $32, which CommitSprites uses to decide which half is showing this frame.

Free the sprite for object slot Y: sprInUse[Y] = 0 and the bit cleared from whichever enable mask SSET put it in. The same shift loop as SSET, so this is SSET written out again with AND/EOR instead of ORA. Nine callers - anything that kills an object comes through here.

SPAWN TICK, run once per pass of the main loop.

First a timer: $43 counts down and reloads with 12 minus twice loopNumber, so the whole spawn system runs FASTER on later loops of the game - that is the only difficulty knob outside the zone data.

Then the pause key check, the camel colour fade, and finally the spawn scan: for each of the eight object types, decrement typeSpawnTimer[type] and when it hits zero call SpawnOneOfType. So the zone template byte tmplSpawnInterval controls how often each creature appears, per type, per zone.

Ends by jumping to $98A9, which runs the per-object update over slots 2-15.

So the test at $9283 always finds sprInUse zero, always takes the sub_929D path, and the shadow arrays at $1F48/$1F58/$1F68/$1F78 are written by nothing.

So this is machinery for sixteen sprites that the game as shipped drives with eight — which is a fact about the program, not about the analysis, and exactly the sort of thing only reading the data settles. Keep the field names: they are correct about what the code would do.

(One consequence for anyone reading further: the frame-1 enable mask sprEnableMaskFrame1 at $1F99 stays whatever CheckOptionsKey and sub_92F6 left in it, and it is ORed into $D015 on odd frames regardless.)

THE COMPLETE ZONE RECORD, 200 bytes. The first 152 are nineteen tables of eight - one row per attribute, one column per creature type - copied wholesale to $1DA0 by LoadZoneTemplates, so the offset here IS the offset from $1DA0 and every tmpl* label is a slice of this:

  +$00 $1DA0 tmplSpawnInterval    ticks between spawns of this type
  +$08 $1DA8 tmplMoveType         0 static, 1 linear, 2 accelerating (dispatch at $993A)
  +$10 $1DB0 tmplAnimFirst        first sprite block of the animation
  +$18 $1DB8 tmplAnimLast         last one; equal to the first means no animation
  +$20 $1DC0 tmplAnimMode         low 6 bits are the frame delay, bits 6 and 7 select ping-pong
  +$28 $1DC8 tmplTypeWhenShot     what it becomes when the bullet hits it
  +$30 $1DD0 tmplTypeWhenExploded what it becomes when the camel hits it
  +$38 $1DD8 tmplNextType         what it becomes when its lifetime runs out; $FF means die
  +$40 $1DE0 tmplSpeedX           sign-magnitude, low 7 bits a countdown
  +$48 $1DE8 tmplSpeedY           same
  +$50 $1DF0 tmplField80          step size added to the position each move
  +$58 $1DF8 tmplSpawnLimit       bit 7 counts against a per-zone cap, bit 6 and the low nibble select the extra behaviour at $9C64
  +$60 $1E00 tmplSpawnX           spawn column, or 0 to mean random
  +$68 $1E08 tmplSpawnY           spawn row, or 0 to mean random
  +$70 $1E10 tmplSpawnMode        0 fixed, $10 random, anything else = place relative to a live object of type (low nibble - 1)
  +$78 $1E18 tmplColour           sprite colour, bit 7 selects multicolour
  +$80 $1E20 tmplLifetime         ticks before it turns into tmplNextType
  +$88 $1E28 tmplScoreValue       low nibble = score digit column, high nibble = how many to add. $15 is 100, $56 is 50, $55 is 500. Zero means shooting it scores nothing and makes no sound
  +$90 $1E30 tmplExplodeLength    how much neutronium an explosion of this type burns

Then eight scalars read by $9CB5 in this order:
  +$98 typeMulticolourMask, +$99 typeYExpandMask, +$9A typeXExpandMask,
  +$9B the object slot limit (8 in 41 zones, 6 in zone 6),
  +$9C the sprite bank index (only ever 0, 2, 4 or 6),
  +$9D $D025, +$9E $D026, +$9F read and discarded.

And finally +$A0..+$C7, the 40-character zone name in screen codes.

Worked example, zone 0 type 7: interval $A1, move type 2, shape $B8 to $B8, spawn mode 7 - so it is placed on top of a live type 6 - score $55 = 500 points, and it turns into type 0 when shot. Type 0 in the same zone scores nothing, so the wave is a chain: the thing worth 500 becomes something worth nothing.

Confirmed multicolour, and it is the zone 30-35 set. Rendered at two bits per pixel — 12 pixels wide instead of 24, four colours — the shapes resolve cleanly: a fish or rocket, a tall box, a diagonal beam. Rendered as hires the same bytes come out dithered #.#. all over, which is the giveaway.

The zone records agree: $D025 and $D026, the two shared sprite multicolour registers, are set per zone from offsets +157 and +158, and every zone using this bank sets them to a real pair. The box is plausibly the portaloo of zone 31, SIDNEY AND THE PORTALAVS.

THE IMAGE ALREADY CONTAINS A BUILT TABLE, and comparing it with the default proves how it got there.

All 208 bytes here are exactly defaultHighScoreTable at $5474 with each byte ANDed with $3F: 119 bytes identical (spaces and digits, which are the same in PETSCII and screen codes) and the other 89 differing by precisely that mask, none differing any other way. That is what InitDefaultHighScores at $545C does when it copies.

So this is not fresh RAM and it is not what LOAD put here. It is the result of $545C having been RUN on the machine the build was saved from - the same story as the assembler source at $5870 and $5F28. The shipped image is a memory dump of a development session, not a clean link.

Structure, from the default: four entries of 52 bytes. "n  0000000    " is 14 characters - rank, two spaces, seven score digits, four spaces - then 38 characters of name. 4 x 52 = 208, which is exactly the $D0 that $C082 saves and $C065 loads.

The names are Jeff Minter placeholder jokes: I LIKE CAMELS REALLY, I GOT NOTHING AGAINST SHEEP EITHER, LLAMAS ARE LLOVELY, 2D SPACE INVADERS RULE THE ZONE OK. They are stored in the code as PETSCII and on screen as screen codes, which is why the file on disk holds screen codes and would look like control characters to anything else reading it.

NEW GAME INIT - and this is where every starting value in the game is set. Reached from $8A3C after the screen row table is built.

Clears about twenty zero page bytes to zero, blanks the border and background, then:
  $1F = 4     the fine scroll offset
  $4A = $12   EIGHTEEN units of neutronium - the full bar
  $4B = 3     drain sub-tick
  $4C = 6     top of the neutronium colour ramp
  $5A = 3     attract scroll state
  $3F = $67   high byte of the zone data pointer, so it starts at $6700 = zone 0
  $57 = 7     zone distance, the default the options screen edits
  $54 = 5     FIVE BEASTS - the starting lives
  $40 = 8     camel colour
  $5D = $5A, $59 = 0, $5C = 0

Then InstallIrqAndVicMode takes the machine over, the bottom five rows ($0720-$07E7) are filled with character $28 in colour 6 - the ground - and the VIC gets multicolour text, background colours and $D018 = $18 for screen $0400 / characters $2000.

So: 5 beasts, 18 neutronium, zone 0, distance 7. Everything else the player sees is derived from the zone record.

Blank the message line: 40 spaces over $0590-$05B7, then fall into ShowCheatModeBanner, which redraws the cheat banner if the cheat is on. Eight callers - anything that finishes with the message line comes through here, and the fall-through rather than a JSR is why the banner survives every clear.

Drag every object with bit 7 of objMoveType set one column to the left, stopping at X = $10. That bit is the with-the-scroll flag: objects that belong to the terrain move with it, objects that fly do not. Called once every other frame from the raster work phase at $8C20, which is the same cadence the terrain scrolls at.

Push all sixteen object positions into the sprite shadow registers through WriteSpritePosition. Called first thing in CommitSprites, so the shadow registers are always one full pass behind the object updates - which is what stops a sprite being torn between its old X and its new Y.

THE TUNE, measured rather than guessed. Summing the duration byte of every pair up to the $FF terminator:

  voice 1  $6000-$6231  281 pairs  636 ticks  23 distinct notes, indices 33-64
  voice 2  $6320-$64B3  202 pairs  636 ticks  19 distinct notes, indices 33-63
  voice 3  $65A0-$66F5  171 pairs  604 ticks  15 distinct notes, indices 19-43

Voices 1 and 2 come to EXACTLY the same total, which is what a three-part arrangement of one piece looks like and would not happen by accident. Voice 3 is 604 and then rests, so it is the bass line and it stops before the end. The first 38 pairs of all three voices are byte-identical to voice 1, so the piece opens in unison and splits.

Speed: the player runs once per call of CommitSprites, which on the game path is once a frame, and the tempo divider $10/$11 is 7. So a tick is about 0.14 s and the whole tune is around 90 seconds.

The note table it indexes is a true equal-tempered scale - adjacent entries are in ratio 1.0595 and index 12 is exactly twice index 0, 536 against 1072 - but it is not tuned to concert pitch. Index 0 is 536 * 985248 / 16777216 = 31.5 Hz, which sits between B0 at 30.87 and C1 at 32.70, so the whole table is about a third of a semitone sharp of B or two thirds flat of C. Calling any note here by a letter name means choosing which.

Four sprite shapes for the landing squash, CE CF CF CE, indexed 1-based by jumpVelocity counting 4 down to 1. The base operand is $9564, which is the RTS of the routine above - the same one-below-the-table trick the star seed tables use at $8A0D.

One large sprite sheet, ~288 standard 64-byte hi-res C64 sprites (24x21) back to back, from $0801 to $4FFF -- nothing in the code reached so far references it (no root existed before this claim; find_instructions on the VIC sprite-pointer range $07F8-$07FF and on STA $D000-$D010 turns up nothing yet, and it explicitly reports several indirect/computed-address writes it cannot resolve, so the code that actually points the VIC at a sprite number almost certainly lives in the still-undecoded $5E00-$87FD span). Visually (rendered in 16-wide grid chunks): recognisable camels in several walk/leg positions, small flying/aircraft-like enemies, falling parachute figures, devil/pitchfork and skeleton figures, a robot, the digits 0-9 and some letters, and a band roughly a third of the way through that renders as visual noise in this hi-res view -- possibly debris/explosion-particle sprites that are just genuinely busy-looking, possibly something not meant to be read as a plain hi-res sprite (multicolour mode, or a different frame boundary); not resolved. Could not tie any specific sprite index to a name (camel/enemy/digit-N) because the selecting code has not been found yet -- recorded only the visual grouping, not an index mapping.

One byte per object slot (X, up to at least 16 slots -- sub_8B20 zeroes 16 of them at init). Holds the type/kind index of whatever occupies slot X, written by spawn_object_from_template ($9772) as TYA;STA dat_1D10,X right after copying that type's template fields. Read back all over the object-AI code ($9744,$97CB.. through $9C6B) as LDA/LDY dat_1D10,X to fetch Y = type, then Y indexes a further per-type table (e.g. dat_1DF8,Y) -- a two-level indirection: object slot -> type -> per-type property. This is the central "one thing refers to another" relation in the game logic.

Per-object-slot byte (indexed by X, same slot numbering as obj_type at $1D10). Bit 7 is tested alone in several places (e.g. sub_9413: AND #$80) as an on/off flag; the low 7 bits, masked with AND #$7F, are doubled and used as the index into obj_behavior_jumptable ($9933) by sub_993A -- so this byte packs a flag and a behaviour selector together. Same AND #$7F / AND #$80 packing shows up on dat_1D60 and dat_1DF8 too -- a recurring one-flag-plus-7-bit-value convention across several of these per-object tables, not something the model here has a bitfield vocabulary for beyond this comment.

Copies 2048 bytes ($0800-$0FFF) from a source selected by bank_copy_ptr_tbl ($502F/$5030), indexed by X = zero page $02 as set by the caller before the JSR. Destination is fixed. Looks like a bank-switcher swapping some 2K asset (font or HUD graphics bank) into a shared work area; see the comment on bank_copy_ptr_tbl for why the exact table layout is not pinned down.

Read by sub_5007 (LDX from zp $02, then LDA dat_502F,X / LDA dat_5030,X to build a source pointer, then copies 2048 bytes to $0800-$0FFF). Only 1 byte of dat_502F and 11 of dat_5030 are visible in this gap; if read as (lo=dat_502F[X], hi=dat_5030[X]) with X stepping by 1, dat_5030 bytes 10,00,18,00,40,00,48,00,50,00,58 look like six little-endian 16-bit source addresses ($0010,$0018,$0040,$0048,$0050,$0058) rather than six separate lo/hi pairs looked up by a doubled index -- but this is read from the shape of the copy loop, not confirmed by seeing a caller set X, so treat the exact indexing scheme as unresolved.
HUD line, decodes (screen-code) to a string ending in BEASTS REMAINING, one non-letter glyph byte, then a trailing 0. The trailing 0 is presumably overwritten at runtime with the live beast count.

HUD line, decodes to STAND BY YOUR BEAST, one non-letter glyph byte, then PLAYER ONE. That same glyph code is reused in msg_beasts_extinct and msg_enter_your_name below. The trailing ONE is patched to TWO for player 2 by suffix_two_patch_a, copied by sub_5143.

Copied by sub_5143 (LDX#3; loop LDA suffix_two_patch_a,X / STA dat_05AE,X / DEX / BNE) over the tail of msg_stand_by_player's copy in the work buffer when zp location cur_player == 2. Only bytes 1-3 (TWO) are actually written; byte 0 (a space) is never copied since the loop stops at X==0.

Nothing calls this in the code reached so far, hence the missing root -- but it is unambiguous: LDX#0/LDA#$20/STA $5E00,X/INX/BNE fills all 256 bytes of $5E00-$5EFF with spaces, then LDA highscore_entry_1,X / AND #$3F / STA $5E00,X for X=0..207 copies the 208-byte default high-score table (highscore_entry_1..4 at $5474) into it, converting each byte from PETSCII/ASCII (the table encoding, letters 0x41-0x5A) to screen-code (0x01-0x1A) by masking the top two bits.
